issues.legal_issue: A valid sale of mortgaged property by the mortgagor to the mortgagee in possession can end the mortgage estate and change the character of the mortgagee’s possession into possession as owner.
material_facts: The property was subject to a mortgage with possession.
The mortgagors later sold the property to the mortgagees by a registered sale deed.
The mortgagees claimed possession as owners under that sale.
issues.conclusion: As between the mortgagors and the purchasers, the sale was valid and transferred title; possession under the sale could become adverse if it continued for the statutory period, subject to the rights arising from the earlier sale agreement.
issues.legal_principle: A mortgagee in possession cannot unilaterally make possession adverse merely by asserting ownership. But a mortgagor may sell the mortgaged property to the mortgagee, ending the mortgage estate and converting possession into possession as owner. If that possession continues for the statutory period, it may ripen into title. The Court relied on Subbaiya Pandaram v. Mohamad Mustapha Maracayar, Dagadabhai v. Sakharam, and Bogilal v. Ratanlal for the principle that a decree that does not actually interrupt possession does not change its character.

rule.if: mortgagee_holds_possession_under_mortgage and mortgagor_sells_property_to_mortgagee and sale_is_valid_between_them and no_enforceable_prior_contract_right_against_purchaser and possession_continues_for_limitation_period

predicates.mortgagee_holds_possession_under_mortgag: The person claiming ownership is in possession of the property under a mortgage.
predicates.mortgagor_sells_property_to_mortgagee: The mortgagor sells the mortgaged property to the mortgagee.
predicates.sale_is_valid_between_them: The sale is binding as between the mortgagor and the mortgagee.
predicates.no_enforceable_prior_contract_right_agai: No person has an enforceable right under an earlier contract that limits the purchaser’s ability to hold the property adversely to that person.
predicates.possession_continues_for_limitation_peri: The purchaser continues in possession as owner for the period required for adverse possession.

issues.definition: When a mortgagee in possession acquires the property by a sale binding between the parties, and no enforceable prior contractual right limits the purchaser’s possession, continued possession as owner for the required period results in title by adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser with notice of an enforceable earlier contract to sell holds the property for the benefit of the earlier contract purchaser to the extent needed to enforce that contract, so possession is not adverse to that beneficiary.
material_facts: The coparceners agreed to sell the properties to the prospective purchasers subject to the existing mortgage.
The coparceners later sold the properties to the mortgagees’ sons, who knew of the earlier agreement; the defence that the later purchase was without notice was rejected.
The earlier contract purchasers obtained a decree for specific performance.
The later purchasers’ possession was asserted under the later sale, but remained subject to the earlier purchasers’ right to specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The later purchasers’ possession was not adverse to the earlier contract purchasers, and the redemption suit was not barred by limitation on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 91 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, a person who acquires property with notice of an existing contract capable of specific performance must hold it for the contract beneficiary to the extent needed to give effect to the contract. Section 40, paragraph 2, of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, makes the relevant contractual obligation enforceable against a transferee who takes with notice. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that a contract for sale does not itself create an interest in the property. Section 3 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, recognises the relevant obligation and fiduciary character. Relying on Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, Gafur v. Bhikaji Govind, Sathiraju v. Venkanna, and Appa Rao v. Veeranna, the Court held that a sale to a subsequent purchaser with notice is not void but is subject to the earlier purchaser’s right of specific performance.

rule.if: redemption_suit and enforceable_prior_sale_contract_exists and later_purchaser_acquires_property_with_notice and specific_performance_right_exists

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding seeks redemption of mortgaged property and possession.
predicates.enforceable_prior_sale_contract_exists: A prior contract to sell the property exists and is enforceable by specific performance.
predicates.later_purchaser_acquires_property_with_n: A subsequent purchaser acquires the property knowing of the prior contract.
predicates.specific_performance_right_exists: The prior contract purchaser has a right to specific performance against the subsequent purchaser.

issues.definition: In a redemption suit, when a subsequent purchaser takes with notice of an enforceable prior sale contract and the contract beneficiary has a right to specific performance, the purchaser’s possession does not bar the beneficiary’s claim as adverse possession.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser’s failure to join as a conveying party to a deed executed under a specific-performance decree does not make possession adverse where the purchaser was directed to convey and attested the deed with knowledge of the beneficiary’s title.
material_facts: The specific-performance decree directed all defendants, including the later purchaser, to execute the conveyance.
The later purchaser was not made a conveying party to the deed executed through the court but signed it as an attesting witness.
By attesting the deed, the later purchaser was made aware that title was being conveyed to the earlier contract purchasers and that the later purchasers retained only the mortgage-related right.
issues.conclusion: The later purchaser’s status as an attesting witness rather than a conveying party did not alter the conclusion that possession was not adverse to the earlier contract purchasers; the redemption suit was therefore not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand states that the appropriate form of a specific-performance decree is for the vendor and subsequent purchaser to join in the conveyance. However, where the decree required the subsequent purchaser to join, the purchaser’s omission from the conveying parties did not change the character of possession in the circumstances here; attestation made the purchaser aware of the conveyance and the beneficiary’s rights. This is consistent with the fiduciary obligation arising under section 91 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and paragraph 2 of section 40 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

rule.if: redemption_suit and specific_performance_decree_requires_purchaser_to_join_conveyance and purchaser_only_attests_deed and purchaser_knows_beneficiary_title

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding seeks redemption of mortgaged property and possession.
predicates.specific_performance_decree_requires_pur: A decree for specific performance requires the subsequent purchaser to join in conveying the property.
predicates.purchaser_only_attests_deed: The subsequent purchaser signs the conveyance only as an attesting witness and not as a conveying party.
predicates.purchaser_knows_beneficiary_title: The subsequent purchaser knows that title is being conveyed to the contract beneficiary and knows the limits of the purchaser’s remaining rights.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance decree requires a subsequent purchaser to join the conveyance, the purchaser’s attestation of the deed with knowledge of the beneficiary’s title leaves possession nonadverse to that beneficiary.
